Easy.q: Which organizational strategy is the industry standard for Playwright test files to ensure scalability and parallelization?
options: Group related tests logically in folders based on features or domains
Put all tests in a single massive file
Keep all tests in the root directory without folders
Use random file names to avoid conflicts
Easy.a: Group related tests logically in folders based on features or domains
Easy.explanation: Grouping tests logically makes the test suite maintainable and easier to scale.
Easy.scenario: Your team is arguing about how to structure a new repository containing 500 E2E tests for a massive e-commerce application.

Medium.scenario: You have a suite of 500 tests. You want to run only the tests related to the 'checkout' flow without manually passing file paths.
Medium.q: What is the standard architectural approach?
options: Use test.describe('checkout') and run `npx playwright test -g "checkout"`.
Put all checkout tests in a single checkout.spec.ts file and hardcode the path.
Use the --only CLI flag.
Comment out the other 450 tests before running.
Medium.a: Use test.describe('checkout') and run `npx playwright test -g "checkout"`.
Medium.explanation: The -g (grep) flag allows you to run tests matching a specific title or tag across your entire codebase, making it the standard way to run logical suites.

Hard.scenario: An enterprise team is testing three distinct environments (QA, Staging, Prod) and uses a playwright.config.ts file.
Hard.q: What is the most scalable way to handle environment-specific variables like Base URLs?
options: Use dotenv to load environment variables and reference process.env.BASE_URL in the config's use block.
Hardcode the URLs directly into every .spec.ts file.
Create three separate config files (qa.config.ts, prod.config.ts) and duplicate the settings.
Use a global setup file to write the URL to a text file on disk.
Hard.a: Use dotenv to load environment variables and reference process.env.BASE_URL in the config's use block.
Hard.explanation: Injecting configurations via environment variables is a 12-Factor App best practice. It prevents hardcoded secrets and allows CI/CD pipelines to easily swap configurations without touching the code.

Easy.q: How can you logically group these tests in the file so that the HTML report visually separates them into distinct sections?
options: To group related tests and share hooks/configuration
To execute an individual test assertion
To launch a new browser instance
To pause the test execution
Easy.a: To group related tests and share hooks/configuration
Easy.explanation: test.describe blocks allow you to logically group tests and share before/after hooks among them.
Easy.scenario: You have a test file with 15 tests. The first 5 test the 'Checkout' feature, and the last 10 test 'User Settings'.

Medium.q: How many times will the beforeEach hook execute during this run?
options: 1 time (before test A).
2 times (before test A and test B).
0 times.
It runs once before the describe block starts.
Medium.explanation: Hooks declared inside a test.describe block are strictly scoped to the tests within that block. Test 'B' exists outside the block and will not trigger the hook.

Hard.q: Assuming the global config does not enforce fullyParallel, what does this specific configuration block do?
options: It overrides the default sequential file execution, forcing tests A and B to run concurrently in separate worker processes.
It forces tests A and B to run simultaneously in the same Node.js thread using Promise.all().
It tells the CI server to spawn another container.
It ignores any beforeEach hooks to save time.
Hard.a: It overrides the default sequential file execution, forcing tests A and B to run concurrently in separate worker processes.
Hard.explanation: By default, tests inside a single file run sequentially in the same worker. Using mode: 'parallel' inside a describe block breaks the tests apart, distributing them to separate OS-level worker processes to speed up execution.

Medium.q: Why is keeping setup hooks lightweight an important architectural pattern?
options: To prevent test flakiness
Because Playwright requires it
To make tests slower
It is optional

Hard.q: Which setup hook anti-pattern causes race conditions when `fullyParallel` is enabled?
options: Using global state across tests
Using test.beforeEach
Using web-first assertions
Using page.goto
Hard.scenario: You are auditing a failing test suite focused on this module's core topic.

Easy.scenario: Your test suite has 50 tests. 45 of them start by filling in a login form with the exact same selectors and credentials.
Easy.q: What happens when the engineering team adds a 'Company Name' field to the login page?
options: You must manually open 45 tests and update the code in every single one
Playwright automatically updates them using AI
The tests will continue passing because Playwright ignores new fields
The pipeline deletes the tests
Easy.a: You must manually open 45 tests and update the code in every single one
Easy.explanation: Code duplication leads to severe maintenance overhead. A single UI change breaks everything and requires an arduous refactoring effort.

Easy.code:
test('A', async () => { await login(); });
test('B', async () => { await login(); });
Easy.q: What architectural concept aims to resolve this exact duplication?
options: Page Object Model (POM) and Fixtures
Serial execution mode
Web-first assertions
Using global variables
Easy.explanation: Abstracting repeated logic into POMs or custom fixtures is the standard enterprise approach to achieving DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) code.

Medium.scenario: A junior SDET proposes moving all shared logic into a single massive `test.beforeEach` block at the top of a huge test file to avoid duplication.
Medium.q: Why might this be an anti-pattern?
options: It forces tests that don't need all that setup to run it anyway, increasing execution time and coupling
beforeEach hooks are forbidden in Playwright
It breaks parallelization
It throws a syntax error
Medium.a: It forces tests that don't need all that setup to run it anyway, increasing execution time and coupling
Medium.explanation: While `beforeEach` is good for local setup, dumping *everything* there creates monolithic, slow tests. Fixtures are preferred because they only execute when explicitly requested by a test.

Medium.scenario: You are auditing a test repository for duplication code smells.
Medium.q: Which of the following are strong indicators of the 'Duplication Problem'? (Select all that apply)
options: The exact same CSS selector string appears in 10 different files
Multiple tests share the same 15 lines of setup code
Every test starts with `await page.goto('/')`
All tests use `expect()`
a: The exact same CSS selector string appears in 10 different files
Multiple tests share the same 15 lines of setup code
Medium.explanation: Duplicated strings (locators) and heavy duplicated logic (setup) are massive code smells. A single `page.goto` is acceptable, and `expect` is mandatory.

Hard.scenario: You have successfully abstracted your login logic into a reusable utility class. However, tests running in parallel are now sporadically failing with authentication errors.
Hard.q: What architectural mistake likely caused this during refactoring?
options: The utility class was instantiated globally outside the test blocks, causing workers to share state and overwrite each other's tokens
The utility class used async/await
Playwright cannot handle custom classes in parallel
The timeout was too low
Hard.a: The utility class was instantiated globally outside the test blocks, causing workers to share state and overwrite each other's tokens
Hard.explanation: When removing duplication, engineers often mistakenly put shared instances in the global file scope. Playwright requires strict isolation; classes must be instantiated *inside* the test block or passed via fixtures.
